content.content:
1	Many liquid handling installations add a small, accurately measured quantity of a concentrate to a much larger stream of a carrier liquid that is already flowing in a pipe. The concentrate may be aggressive, staining, strongly coloured, biologically active, or simply expensive, and the quantity that must be added is small in comparison with the carrier flow. The addition therefore has to be made repeatably, without measuring the concentrate by eye, and without allowing the concentrate to reach any part of the installation other than the carrier stream itself.
2	
3	Two practical difficulties dominate this kind of dosing. The first is separation of the two liquids upstream of the point of addition. A dosing device sits between a concentrate source and a pressurised carrier line, and any path that momentarily connects the two allows carrier liquid to be forced back into the concentrate source or allows concentrate to migrate into the carrier line at a time when no dose is called for. Devices that rely on separately actuated shut-off elements to keep the two sides apart depend on those elements being commanded in the correct order, so a control fault, a lost signal, or a slow-acting element can open both sides at once.
4	
5	The second difficulty is residue. The surfaces that the concentrate touches, in particular the port through which it enters the metering volume and the seat of the check element through which the dose leaves, retain a film of concentrate after the dose has been delivered. That film drips into the carrier stream between doses, so the quantity actually added is not the quantity that was measured. It also dries, crystallises, or reacts on the wetted surfaces, so that a valve which was accurate when new drifts, sticks, or seizes in service. The usual remedy is to break the valve out of the line and clean it by hand, which takes the installation out of service and exposes the person doing the work to the concentrate. Where a rinse is provided at all, it is commonly a separate operation that has to be commanded after the dose, and it therefore depends on an operator or a controller performing an extra step at the right moment.
6	
7	Dose selection presents a further difficulty. Adjustable dosing devices are often set by a screw or by an electronically stored value. A screw setting can be lost during cleaning and gives no indication of what was set. An electronic setting requires power, a sensor and a display at the valve, which is unwelcome in wet, washdown or hazardous locations, and it tells the operator only what the controller believes rather than what the mechanism will actually deliver.
8	
9	There remains a need for an inline metering valve in which the separation of the concentrate from the carrier liquid is enforced by the geometry of the moving parts rather than by the order in which external commands arrive, in which the surfaces wetted by the concentrate are rinsed by the carrier liquid as an unavoidable part of the return of the metering element, and in which the selected dose is both retained and displayed mechanically.
10

FIG. 1 shows an inline liquid metering valve 10 having a cylindrical housing 12 with an inlet 14 at one axial end and an outlet 16 at the opposite axial end, a metering sleeve 18 fixed within the housing 12, a cartridge 64 retained in the housing 12 by a threaded end cap 66, and a transparent window 52 in the housing 12.

The inline liquid metering valve 10 is connected in a line that already carries a flowing carrier liquid. Carrier liquid enters at the inlet 14, passes along the housing 12, and leaves at the outlet 16. That flow is the main flow into which each dose of concentrate is delivered, and it is also the flow that rinses the valve. The metering sleeve 18 is spaced radially inward from the inner surface of the housing 12 over part of its length.

FIG. 2 shows the metering sleeve 18 defining a dose chamber 20, a concentrate port 22 opening into the dose chamber 20 and a carrier-liquid admission port 24 opening into the dose chamber 20. FIG. 2 further shows an upstream sealing land 30 and a downstream sealing land 32 joined by a reduced-diameter waist 34 in the fill position, and a one-way outlet valve 38.

The dose chamber 20 is cylindrical. The concentrate port 22 is a radial port through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and is connected in use to a concentrate source. The carrier-liquid admission port 24 passes through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 at an axial position downstream of the concentrate port 22, and admits carrier liquid to the dose chamber 20. The metering sleeve 18 further defines a flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20.

The upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 are axially spaced from one another on the piston 28 and are joined by the reduced-diameter waist 34. Each sealing land bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20, while the waist 34 stands clear of that wall. A piston rod 36 extends from the piston 28 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 and is arranged to be driven through a stroke and a return stroke. The one-way outlet valve 38 is arranged to pass liquid from the dose chamber 20 toward the outlet 16 and to prevent flow in the opposite direction.

In the fill position the waist 34 connects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20, and the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolate the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. Concentrate accordingly passes from the concentrate source through the concentrate port 22 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume of concentrate, the extent of which is fixed by the travel then permitted to the piston 28. Throughout the fill position the carrier-liquid path is closed to the concentrate, because the downstream sealing land 32 overlies the carrier-liquid admission port 24 while the upstream sealing land 30 closes the dose chamber 20 on the other side of the waist 34.

Movement of the piston 28 toward the discharge position closes the concentrate port 22 before the downstream sealing land 32 uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port 24. The upstream sealing land 30 arrives at the concentrate port 22 and shuts it while the downstream sealing land 32 is still overlying the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Only after that has happened does continued travel of the piston 28 carry the downstream sealing land 32 clear of the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Carrier liquid then enters through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume of concentrate in the dose chamber 20 and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16, where it joins the main flow.

The two radial rinse openings 62 pass through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and connect the annular rinse channel 60 to the dose chamber 20. The flush poppet 58 is normally closed and is connected to the flush bypass 26. Near the end of the return stroke, the follower pin 44 reaches the flush poppet 58 and opens it. Carrier liquid then flows from the inlet 14 through the annular rinse channel 60, through the two radial rinse openings 62 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 to the outlet 16. The piston 28 is then returned toward the fill position. During the return, the flexible lip 56 on the upstream sealing land 30 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20, and the follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36 opens the normally closed flush poppet 58. The valve is thereby left charged, rinsed and set, ready for the following cycle.

input.summary:
Authority for this review is the disclosure text, which is reproduced verbatim as the single USER message in input/conversation.md; there is no further USER matter. input/brief.md supplied only the title, applicant/inventor name, the two "Not applicable." statements, and terminology to preserve, all of which the draft honours.

The application body traces cleanly. Every limitation of claims 1-20, and substantially every sentence of 06-summary.md and 08-detailed-description.md, maps to an exact affirmative passage: housing/inlet/outlet ("a cylindrical housing with an inlet at one axial end and an outlet at the opposite axial end"), metering sleeve and its four defined features, the two-land/waist piston and the ordered port closure ("closes the concentrate port before the downstream land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port"), the one-way outlet valve discharge, the geometry-enforced separation ("The ordering of the port edges and lands prevents the concentrate source from communicating directly with the carrier-liquid inlet"), the flexible lip wipe, the follower-pin-opened flush poppet, the annular rinse channel, the two radial rinse openings directed across the concentrate port and the one-way outlet valve, poppet closure before the waist reconnects, the index collar with helical cam groove, one increment per full stroke, three axial stop faces, spring-biased detent in one of three recesses, the transparent window showing one of three numerals, and the cartridge retained by a threaded end cap. Generalising "two radial rinse openings" to "at least one rinse opening" in claims 1 and 13 is a permitted narrowing-to-broadening consistent with the source. The Background is prior-art characterisation and is out of scope for source tracing here. No drafting notes, placeholders, open questions or unresolved alternatives remain anywhere in the draft, no numeral is used for two different parts, all 29 numerals in numerals.md appear on a figure, and no application text attempts to justify a renderer's outline choice with "by way of example" or "any closed outline" language. The abstract is a single paragraph of about 145 words.

The defects are concentrated in the figure briefs, where functional-surface geometry has been verbalized beyond the source. Seven items are untraced substantive matter, reported as critical:

1. The annular rinse channel is verbalized as open at its downstream end directly into the housing interior that leads to the outlet, and open at the left to the inlet interior (FIG-1 and FIG-3). The source gives exactly one route - channel, rinse openings, flush bypass, outlet - and no direct channel-to-outlet path.
2. The one-way outlet valve is verbalized as a ball resting on a conical seat that widens downward, in a passage rising through the upper sleeve band (FIG-2, FIG-3). The source says only "a one-way outlet valve"; taper plus contact topology are substantive even for a schematic.
3. The flush poppet is verbalized as a conical head against a conical seat at a turn in the bypass, with a stem routed leftward through the annular rinse channel above the sleeve and past the sleeve's left end (FIG-3). The source says only that the follower pin opens a normally closed flush poppet connected to the flush bypass.
4. The helical cam groove's runout direction is verbalized ("from the lower left of that surface to the upper right"), fixing the hand of the helix, which the source does not disclose (FIG-4).
5. The three axial stop faces are verbalized as "three steps of increasing projection rightward" on the collar's right end face, fixing a monotonic ordering and an end location the source does not give (FIG-4).
6. The numbered rinse opening's axial position relative to the piston lands and its aim angle are verbalized ("lies right of the right portion of the piston, clear of both portions, and is aimed up and left toward the concentrate port"), which is untraced and is also internally incoherent: the same brief shows the concentrate port covered by the left (upstream) land, with the piston body between the opening and the port it is said to be aimed at (FIG-3).
7. The flexible lip's flare direction is verbalized ("extends up and left to the upper bore wall"), an orientation of a functional wiping face that the source does not give (FIG-3).

Two internal-consistency defects are reported as major: the index collar is placed in two irreconcilable positions - a ring midway along the housing beneath the window in FIG-1 versus a collar whose left part overhangs the sleeve's left end where the follower pin engages the groove in FIG-3/FIG-4 - and FIG-1 additionally seats that ring inside the very annular gap FIG-3 identifies as the annular rinse channel; and FIG-1 shows the piston rod terminating blind short of a closed end cap, which contradicts 08-detailed-description.md's statement that the rod "is arranged to be driven through a stroke and a return stroke."

Four minor items complete the ledger: the concentrate-source tube verbalized as crossing the annular gap and the housing wall (untraced connection topology, FIG-2/FIG-3); the spring-biased detent verbalized as a ball seated in a rounded notch under a coil spring (contact topology, FIG-4); numeral 36 recited in the description's FIG. 3 sentence but absent from FIG-3's numeral list; group numerals 46, 50, 54 and 62 named in the plural in numerals.md while each leader targets a single member; and a lack of antecedent basis in claim 9 for "the axial stop face" and "the dose setting numeral."

Per instructions, no rendered images were inspected and no prior-art file was consulted; the art supplied may be incomplete, which does not affect this source-fidelity ledger. Every fix below is a deletion or a genericising rewrite confined to the figure brief, or a clean claim/table correction; none adds a speculative shape or optional embodiment to the application text.

findings.title: Annular rinse channel verbalized as opening directly into the housing interiors at both ends
findings.where: figures/FIG-1.md (Geometry, sleeve bullet); figures/FIG-3.md (Geometry, second bullet)
findings.detail: Both briefs give the annular rinse channel open flow boundaries that the source does not disclose: a direct opening from the channel's downstream end into the housing interior leading to the outlet, and an open left end to the housing interior toward the inlet. The disclosed flush route is a single ordered path - annular rinse channel, then the two radial rinse openings, then the flush bypass, then the outlet. Verbalizing a second, permanently open path around the sleeve to the outlet is a substantive flow-path assertion (it would let carrier liquid bypass the sleeve continuously, independently of the flush poppet) and it is untraced. This is not a depiction convention: it is a flow boundary, not an outline.
findings.evidence: FIG-1: "so that a clear gap is visible above and below it over part of its length, from a position right of the end cap to the right-hand end of the sleeve, which stands short of the end wall, the gap opening at that end into the housing interior that leads to the outlet." FIG-3: "The clear gap between the sleeve and outer bands, above and below, is one annular rinse channel, open at the left to the housing interior toward the inlet and open at its right end, beyond the sleeve's right end, to the housing interior that leads to the outlet." Nearest source passage, which shows the gap: "Carrier liquid flows through an annular rinse channel between the sleeve and housing, through two radial rinse openings directed across the concentrate port and the one-way outlet valve, and then through the flush bypass to the outlet." The disclosure contains no affirmative statement that the rinse channel discharges directly to the outlet or opens to the housing interior at either end.

In figures/FIG-3.md, replace the second Geometry bullet with: "The clear gap between the sleeve and outer bands, above and below, is the annular rinse channel, supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet end of the housing; its ends are not shown open to the housing interior."

data.summary:
Authority for this review is the disclosure text, which is reproduced verbatim as the single USER message in input/conversation.md; there is no further USER matter. input/brief.md supplied only the title, applicant/inventor name, the two "Not applicable." statements, and terminology to preserve, all of which the draft honours.

The application body traces cleanly. Every limitation of claims 1-20, and substantially every sentence of 06-summary.md and 08-detailed-description.md, maps to an exact affirmative passage: housing/inlet/outlet ("a cylindrical housing with an inlet at one axial end and an outlet at the opposite axial end"), metering sleeve and its four defined features, the two-land/waist piston and the ordered port closure ("closes the concentrate port before the downstream land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port"), the one-way outlet valve discharge, the geometry-enforced separation ("The ordering of the port edges and lands prevents the concentrate source from communicating directly with the carrier-liquid inlet"), the flexible lip wipe, the follower-pin-opened flush poppet, the annular rinse channel, the two radial rinse openings directed across the concentrate port and the one-way outlet valve, poppet closure before the waist reconnects, the index collar with helical cam groove, one increment per full stroke, three axial stop faces, spring-biased detent in one of three recesses, the transparent window showing one of three numerals, and the cartridge retained by a threaded end cap. Generalising "two radial rinse openings" to "at least one rinse opening" in claims 1 and 13 is a permitted narrowing-to-broadening consistent with the source. The Background is prior-art characterisation and is out of scope for source tracing here. No drafting notes, placeholders, open questions or unresolved alternatives remain anywhere in the draft, no numeral is used for two different parts, all 29 numerals in numerals.md appear on a figure, and no application text attempts to justify a renderer's outline choice with "by way of example" or "any closed outline" language. The abstract is a single paragraph of about 145 words.

The defects are concentrated in the figure briefs, where functional-surface geometry has been verbalized beyond the source. Seven items are untraced substantive matter, reported as critical:

1. The annular rinse channel is verbalized as open at its downstream end directly into the housing interior that leads to the outlet, and open at the left to the inlet interior (FIG-1 and FIG-3). The source gives exactly one route - channel, rinse openings, flush bypass, outlet - and no direct channel-to-outlet path.
2. The one-way outlet valve is verbalized as a ball resting on a conical seat that widens downward, in a passage rising through the upper sleeve band (FIG-2, FIG-3). The source says only "a one-way outlet valve"; taper plus contact topology are substantive even for a schematic.
3. The flush poppet is verbalized as a conical head against a conical seat at a turn in the bypass, with a stem routed leftward through the annular rinse channel above the sleeve and past the sleeve's left end (FIG-3). The source says only that the follower pin opens a normally closed flush poppet connected to the flush bypass.
4. The helical cam groove's runout direction is verbalized ("from the lower left of that surface to the upper right"), fixing the hand of the helix, which the source does not disclose (FIG-4).
5. The three axial stop faces are verbalized as "three steps of increasing projection rightward" on the collar's right end face, fixing a monotonic ordering and an end location the source does not give (FIG-4).
6. The numbered rinse opening's axial position relative to the piston lands and its aim angle are verbalized ("lies right of the right portion of the piston, clear of both portions, and is aimed up and left toward the concentrate port"), which is untraced and is also internally incoherent: the same brief shows the concentrate port covered by the left (upstream) land, with the piston body between the opening and the port it is said to be aimed at (FIG-3).
7. The flexible lip's flare direction is verbalized ("extends up and left to the upper bore wall"), an orientation of a functional wiping face that the source does not give (FIG-3).

Two internal-consistency defects are reported as major: the index collar is placed in two irreconcilable positions - a ring midway along the housing beneath the window in FIG-1 versus a collar whose left part overhangs the sleeve's left end where the follower pin engages the groove in FIG-3/FIG-4 - and FIG-1 additionally seats that ring inside the very annular gap FIG-3 identifies as the annular rinse channel; and FIG-1 shows the piston rod terminating blind short of a closed end cap, which contradicts 08-detailed-description.md's statement that the rod "is arranged to be driven through a stroke and a return stroke."

Four minor items complete the ledger: the concentrate-source tube verbalized as crossing the annular gap and the housing wall (untraced connection topology, FIG-2/FIG-3); the spring-biased detent verbalized as a ball seated in a rounded notch under a coil spring (contact topology, FIG-4); numeral 36 recited in the description's FIG. 3 sentence but absent from FIG-3's numeral list; group numerals 46, 50, 54 and 62 named in the plural in numerals.md while each leader targets a single member; and a lack of antecedent basis in claim 9 for "the axial stop face" and "the dose setting numeral."

Per instructions, no rendered images were inspected and no prior-art file was consulted; the art supplied may be incomplete, which does not affect this source-fidelity ledger. Every fix below is a deletion or a genericising rewrite confined to the figure brief, or a clean claim/table correction; none adds a speculative shape or optional embodiment to the application text.
